cves.description: On the BIG-IP system, undisclosed endpoints that contain static non-sensitive information are accessible to an unauthenticated remote attacker through the Configuration utility. (CVE-2025-59268)
cves.impact: This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to the Configuration utility through the BIG-IP management port and/or self IP addresses to access pages that do not contain any device-specific or configuration-related information through undisclosed endpoints. There is no data plane exposure; this is a control plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
Until you can install a fixed version, you can use the following sections as temporary mitigations. These mitigations restrict access to the Configuration utility to only trusted networks or devices, thereby limiting the attack surface.

Block Configuration utility access through self IP addresses
Block Configuration utility access through the management interface

Block Configuration utility access through self IP addresses

You can block all access to the Configuration utility of your BIG-IP system using self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address on the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to block access to the Configuration utility. By default, the Configuration utility listens on TCP port 443. If you modified the default port, ensure that you block access to the alternate port you configured.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to the Configuration utility and iControl REST using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services, including breaking high availability (HA) configurations. For more information, refer to K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K31003634: The Configuration utility of the Single-NIC BIG-IP Virtual Edition now defaults to TCP port 8443
K51358480: The single-NIC BIG-IP VE may erroneously revert to the default management httpd port after a configuration reload

If you must expose port 443 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block Configuration utility access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to F5 products to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13309: Restricting access to the Configuration utility by source IP address (11.x - 17.x)

cves.description: A vulnerability exists in an undisclosed iControl REST and BIG-IP TMOS Shell (tmsh) command that may allow an authenticated attacker with at least the resource administrator role to execute arbitrary system commands with higher privileges. A successful exploit can allow the attacker to cross a security boundary. (CVE-2025-59481)
cves.impact:
In standard deployments, this vulnerability may allow an authenticated attacker with at least resource administrator role privileges and network access to the affected iControl REST endpoint and local access to the affected tmsh command to execute arbitrary system commands with higher privileges and create or delete files through the BIG-IP management port or self IP addresses.

The vulnerability allows the bypass of Appliance mode security on BIG-IP systems by allowing the authenticated attacker with at least resource administrator role privileges to execute arbitrary Advanced Shell (bash) commands with higher privileges. There is no data plane exposure; this is a control plane issue only. There is no Availability impact beyond existing user capabilities.

Note: Appliance mode is enforced by a specific license or may be enabled or disabled for individual Virtual Clustered Multiprocessing (vCMP) guest instances. For more information about Appliance mode, refer to K12815: Overview of Appliance mode.
cves.mitigation:
As this attack is conducted by legitimate, authenticated, administrator role users, there is no viable mitigation that also allows users access to the BIG-IP system. The only mitigation is to remove access for users who are not completely trusted.

Until it is possible to install a fixed version, you can use the following sections as temporary mitigations. These mitigations restrict access to iControl REST to only trusted networks or devices, and to the BIG-IP command line through SSH to only trusted networks or devices, thereby limiting the attack surface.

Block iControl REST access through the self IP address
Block iControl REST access through the management interface
Block SSH access through self IP addresses
Block SSH access through the management interface

Block iControl REST access through the self IP address

You can block all access to the iControl REST interface of your BIG-IP system through self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address in the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to disallow access to iControl REST. By default, iControl REST listens on TCP port 443 or TCP port 8443 on single NIC BIG-IP VE instances. If you modified the default port, ensure that you disallow access to the alternate port you configured.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to the Configuration utility and iControl REST using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services, including breaking high availability (HA) configurations.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K31003634: The Configuration utility of the Single-NIC BIG-IP Virtual Edition now defaults to TCP port 8443
K51358480: The single-NIC BIG-IP VE may erroneously revert to the default management httpd port after a configuration reload

If you must expose port 443 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block iControl REST access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules
K69354049: Use iptables to restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface for Configuration utility and iControl REST services

Block SSH access through self IP addresses

You can block all access to the command line through SSH of your BIG-IP system using self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address on the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to block access to SSH. By default, the SSH service listens on TCP port 22.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to SSH using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system

If you must expose port 22 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block SSH access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to F5 products to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules

cves.description: Flowise is a drag & drop user interface to build a customized large language model flow. In version 3.0.5, Flowise is vulnerable to remote code execution. The CustomMCP node allows users to input configuration settings for connecting to an external MCP server. This node parses the user-provided mcpServerConfig string to build the MCP server configuration. However, during this process, it executes JavaScript code without any security validation. Specifically, inside the convertToValidJSONString function, user input is directly passed to the Function() constructor, which evaluates and executes the input as JavaScript code. Since this runs with full Node.js runtime privileges, it can access dangerous modules such as child_process and fs. This issue has been patched in version 3.0.6. (CVE-2025-59528)

cves.description: When Diffie-Hellman (DH) group Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool curves are configured in an SSL profile's Cipher Rule or Cipher Group, and that profile is applied to a virtual server, undisclosed traffic can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate. (CVE-2025-60016)
cves.impact:
Traffic is disrupted while the TMM process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: This issue affects both Client SSL and Server SSL profiles, as long as they are configured with a Cipher Rule or Cipher Group that includes an ECC Brainpool curve in the DH Groups setting.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability, ensure that ECC Brainpool curves are not selected in the DH Groups setting of the Cipher Rule or Cipher Group associated with the affected SSL profile.

To verify if ECC Brainpool curves are used in any of the cipher rules, review the Local Traffic > Ciphers > Rules page in the BIG-IP Configuration utility.

Alternatively, you can use the following TMOS Shell (tmsh) command to determine if any of the cipher rules are using ECC Brainpool curves:

tmsh
cd /
list ltm cipher rule recursive one-line | grep BRA

If there are cipher rules using ECC Brainpool curves, then you may observe an output similar to the following example:

ltm cipher rule K000137488-rule { cipher DEFAULT description "Elliptic Curve Cryptography Brainpool curves" dh-groups BRAINPOOLP256R1:BRAINPOOLP384R1:BRAINPOOLP256R1TLS13:BRAINPOOLP384R1TLS13 signature-algorithms DEFAULT }

As of version 17.1.0, BIG-IP supports ECC Brainpool curves. For more information, refer to K000137488: How to implement Elliptic Curve Cryptography Brainpool curves in BIG-IP 17.1.x.

To remove ECC Brainpool curves from the affected cipher rule, perform either of the following procedures:

Impact of action: Performing the following procedure should not have a negative impact on your system.

Configuration utility

Log in to the Configuration utility.
Go to Local Traffic > Ciphers > Rules.
Select the name of the affected cipher rule.
Remove the ECC Brainpool curves definition from the DH Groups setting.
Select Update to save the change.

tmsh utility

Log in to the tmsh utility.
Remove the ECC Brainpool curves definition from the dh-groups setting by entering the following tmsh command syntax:

modify /ltm cipher rule <name of cipher rule> dh-groups <none | other Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithms excluding the Brainpool curves>

Save the change by entering the following tmsh command:

save /sys config

Verify the change by entering the following tmsh command syntax:

list /ltm cipher rule <name of cipher rule>

This issue was discovered internally by F5.

cves.description: A Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) vulnerability was found in libblockdev. Generally, the "allow_active" setting in Polkit permits a physically present user to take certain actions based on the session type. Due to the way libblockdev interacts with the udisks daemon, an "allow_active" user on a system may be able escalate to full root privileges on the target host. Normally, udisks mounts user-provided filesystem images with security flags like nosuid and nodev to prevent privilege escalation. However, a local attacker can create a specially crafted XFS image containing a SUID-root shell, then trick udisks into resizing it. This mounts their malicious filesystem with root privileges, allowing them to execute their SUID-root shell and gain complete control of the system. (CVE-2025-6019)

cves.description: CVE-2025-61662 A Use-After-Free vulnerability has been discovered in GRUB's gettext module. This flaw stems from a programming error where the gettext command remains registered in memory after its module is unloaded. An attacker can exploit this condition by invoking the orphaned command, causing the application to access a memory location that is no longer valid. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to cause grub to crash, leading to a Denial of Service. Possible data integrity or confidentiality compromise is not discarded.

cves.description: Improper Resource Shutdown or Release vulnerability in Apache Tomcat. If an error occurred (including exceeding limits) during the processing of a multipart upload, temporary copies of the uploaded parts written to disc were not cleaned up immediately but left for the garbage collection process to delete. Depending on JVM settings, application memory usage and application load, it was possible that space for the temporary copies of uploaded parts would be filled faster than GC cleared it, leading to a denial-of-service (DoS). This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.11, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.46, from 9.0.0.M1 through 9.0.109. The following versions were End of Life (EoL) at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: 8.5.0 though 8.5.100. Other, older, EoL versions may also be affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.12 or later, 10.1.47 or later or 9.0.110 or later which fixes the issue. (CVE-2025-61795)

affected.vulnerable_component: Data Guard Protection Enforcement URL/the bd process

cves.description: When a BIG-IP Advanced WAF or ASM security policy is configured with a URL greater than 1024 characters in length for the Data Guard Protection Enforcement setting, either manually or through the automatic Policy Builder, the bd process can terminate repeatedly. (CVE-2025-61938)
cves.impact: Traffic is disrupted while the bd process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to use the automatic Policy Builder to trigger a long Data Guard Protection Enforcement URL configuration for the security policy and cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the affected BIG-IP Advanced WAF or ASM system. Automatic Policy Builder will learn a URL only if it receives a valid HTTP response when requested. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this vulnerability, you can replace the long URL in the Data Guard Protection Enforcement setting with a wildcard URL. To do so, perform the following procedure:

Impact of action: Performing the following procedure should not have a negative impact on your system.

Log in to the Configuration utility of the affected BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM system as the administrative user.
Go to Security > Application Security > Security Policies > Policies List.
Select the affected security policy.
Select Advanced Protection.
Select Data Guard.
Locate the long URL and select x to remove it.
To replace the long URL, enter a wildcard URL and select Add.
Select Save.
Select Apply Policy.

For more information about the Data Guard feature, refer to the Protecting Sensitive Data with Data Guard chapter of the BIG-IP Application Security Manager: Implementations manual.

Acknowledgments

This issue was discovered internally by F5.

cves.description: A vulnerability exists in the iHealth utility of the TMOS Shell (tmsh) that may allow an authenticated attacker with at least a resource administrator role to bypass tmsh restrictions and gain access to the Advanced Shell (bash). For BIG-IP systems running in Appliance mode, a successful exploit can allow the attacker to cross a security boundary. (CVE-2025-61958)
cves.impact:
The vulnerability allows the bypass of Appliance mode security on BIG-IP systems by allowing the authenticated attacker, with at least resource administrator role privileges and tmsh access, to bypass tmsh restrictions and gain access to bash. There is no Availability impact beyond existing user capabilities.

Appliance mode is enforced by a specific license or may be enabled or disabled for individual Virtual Clustered Multiprocessing (vCMP) guest instances. For more information about Appliance mode, refer to K12815: Overview of Appliance mode.
cves.mitigation:
As this attack is conducted by legitimate, authenticated users, there is no viable mitigation that also allows users access to the BIG-IP system. The only mitigation is to remove access for users who are not completely trusted.

Until it is possible to install a fixed version, you can use the following sections as temporary mitigations. These mitigations restrict access to the BIG-IP tmsh utility through SSH to only trusted networks or devices, thereby limiting the attack surface.

Block SSH access through self IP addresses
Block SSH access through the management interface

Block SSH access through self IP addresses

You can block all access to the tmsh utility through SSH of your BIG-IP system using self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address on the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to block access to SSH. By default, the SSH service listens on TCP port 22.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to SSH using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system

If you must expose port 22 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter

Block SSH access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to F5 products to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules

cves.description: Issue summary: A TLS 1.3 connection using certificate compression can be forced to allocate a large buffer before decompression without checking against the configured certificate size limit.
cves.impact:
summary: An attacker can cause per-connection memory allocations of up to approximately 22 MiB and extra CPU work, potentially leading to service degradation or resource exhaustion (Denial of Service). In affected configurations, the peer-supplied uncompressed certificate length from a CompressedCertificate message is used to grow a heap buffer prior to decompression. This length is not bounded by the max_cert_list setting, which otherwise constrains certificate message sizes. An attacker can exploit this to cause large per-connection allocations followed by handshake failure. No memory corruption or information disclosure occurs. This issue only affects builds where TLS 1.3 certificate compression is compiled in (i.e., not OPENSSL_NO_COMP_ALG) and at least one compression algorithm (brotli, zlib, or zstd) is available, and where the compression extension is negotiated. Both clients receiving a server CompressedCertificate and servers in mutual TLS scenarios receiving a client CompressedCertificate are affected. Servers that do not request client certificates are not vulnerable to client-initiated attacks. Users can mitigate this issue by setting SSL_OP_NO_RX_CERTIFICATE_COMPRESSION to disable receiving compressed certificates. The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4 and 3.3 are not affected by this issue, as the TLS implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary. OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5, 3.4 and 3.3 are vulnerable to this issue. OpenSSL 3.0, 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 are not affected by this issue. (CVE-2025-66199)

Impact

cves.description: urllib3 is a user-friendly HTTP client library for Python. Starting in version 1.0 and prior to 2.6.0, the Streaming API improperly handles highly compressed data. urllib3's streaming API is designed for the efficient handling of large HTTP responses by reading the content in chunks, rather than loading the entire response body into memory at once. When streaming a compressed response, urllib3 can perform decoding or decompression based on the HTTP Content-Encoding header (e.g., gzip, deflate, br, or zstd). The library must read compressed data from the network and decompress it until the requested chunk size is met. Any resulting decompressed data that exceeds the requested amount is held in an internal buffer for the next read operation. The decompression logic could cause urllib3 to fully decode a small amount of highly compressed data in a single operation. This can result in excessive resource consumption (high CPU usage and massive memory allocation for the decompressed data. (CVE-2025-66471)

cves.description: CVE-2025-66614 Improper Input Validation vulnerability. This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.14, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.49, from 9.0.0-M1 through 9.0.112. The following versions were EOL at the time the CVE was created but are known to be affected: 8.5.0 through 8.5.100. Older EOL versions are not affected. Tomcat did not validate that the host name provided via the SNI extension was the same as the host name provided in the HTTP host header field. If Tomcat was configured with more than one virtual host and the TLS configuration for one of those hosts did not require client certificate authentication but another one did, it was possible for a client to bypass the client certificate authentication by sending different host names in the SNI extension and the HTTP host header field. The vulnerability only applies if client certificate authentication is only enforced at the Connector. It does not apply if client certificate authentication is enforced at the web application. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.15 or later, 10.1.50 or later or 9.0.113 or later, which fix the issue.

cves.description: Issue summary: Writing large, newline-free data into a BIO chain using the line-buffering filter where the next BIO performs short writes can trigger a heap-based out-of-bounds write.
cves.impact:
summary: This out-of-bounds write can cause memory corruption which typically results in a crash, leading to Denial of Service for an application. The line-buffering BIO filter (BIO_f_linebuffer) is not used by default in TLS/SSL data paths. In OpenSSL command-line applications, it is typically only pushed onto stdout/stderr on VMS systems. Third-party applications that explicitly use this filter with a BIO chain that can short-write and that write large, newline-free data influenced by an attacker would be affected. However, the circumstances where this could happen are unlikely to be under attacker control, and BIO_f_linebuffer is unlikely to be handling non-curated data controlled by an attacker. For that reason the issue was assessed as Low severity. The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue, as the BIO implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary. OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3, 3.0, 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 are vulnerable to this issue. (CVE-2025-68160)

cves.description: CVE-2025-68183 In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ima: don't clear IMA_DIGSIG flag when setting or removing non-IMA xattr Currently when both IMA and EVM are in fix mode, the IMA signature will be reset to IMA hash if a program first stores IMA signature in security.ima and then writes/removes some other security xattr for the file. For example, on Fedora, after booting the kernel with "ima_appraise=fix evm=fix ima_policy=appraise_tcb" and installing rpm-plugin-ima, installing/reinstalling a package will not make good reference IMA signature generated. Instead IMA hash is generated, # getfattr -m - -d -e hex /usr/bin/bash # file: usr/bin/bash security.ima=0x0404... This happens because when setting security.selinux, the IMA_DIGSIG flag that had been set early was cleared. As a result, IMA hash is generated when the file is closed. Similarly, IMA signature can be cleared on file close after removing security xattr like security.evm or setting/removing ACL. Prevent replacing the IMA file signature with a file hash, by preventing the IMA_DIGSIG flag from being reset. Here's a minimal C reproducer which sets security.selinux as the last step which can also replaced by removing security.evm or setting ACL, #include #include #include #include #include #include int main() { const char* file_path = "/usr/sbin/test_binary"; const char* hex_string = "030204d33204490066306402304"; int length = strlen(hex_string); char* ima_attr_value; int fd; fd = open(file_path, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL, 0644); if (fd == -1) { perror("Error opening file"); return 1; } ima_attr_value = (char*)malloc(length / 2 ); for (int i = 0, j = 0; i < length; i += 2, j++) { sscanf(hex_string + i, "%2hhx", &ima_attr_value[j]); } if (fsetxattr(fd, "security.ima", ima_attr_value, length/2, 0) == -1) { perror("Error setting extended attribute"); close(fd); return 1; } const char* selinux_value= "system_u:object_r:bin_t:s0"; if (fsetxattr(fd, "security.selinux", selinux_value, strlen(selinux_value), 0) == -1) { perror("Error setting extended attribute"); close(fd); return 1; } close(fd); return 0; }

cves.description: Issue summary: When using the low-level OCB API directly with AES-NI or other hardware-accelerated code paths, inputs whose length is not a multiple of 16 bytes can leave the final partial block unencrypted and unauthenticated.
cves.impact:
summary: The trailing 1-15 bytes of a message may be exposed in cleartext on encryption and are not covered by the authentication tag, allowing an attacker to read or tamper with those bytes without detection. The low-level OCB encrypt and decrypt routines in the hardware-accelerated stream path process full 16-byte blocks but do not advance the input/output pointers. The subsequent tail-handling code then operates on the original base pointers, effectively reprocessing the beginning of the buffer while leaving the actual trailing bytes unprocessed. The authentication checksum also excludes the true tail bytes. However, typical OpenSSL consumers using EVP are not affected because the higher-level EVP and provider OCB implementations split inputs so that full blocks and trailing partial blocks are processed in separate calls, avoiding the problematic code path. Additionally, TLS does not use OCB ciphersuites. The vulnerability only affects applications that call the low-level CRYPTO_ocb128_encrypt() or CRYPTO_ocb128_decrypt() functions directly with non-block-aligned lengths in a single call on hardware-accelerated builds. For these reasons the issue was assessed as Low severity. The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3, 3.2, 3.1 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue, as OCB mode is not a FIPS-approved algorithm. OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3, 3.0 and 1.1.1 are vulnerable to this issue. OpenSSL 1.0.2 is not affected by this issue. (CVE-2025-69418)

cves.description: Issue summary: Calling PKCS12_get_friendlyname() function on a maliciously crafted PKCS#12 file with a BMPString (UTF-16BE) friendly name containing non-ASCII BMP code point can trigger a one byte write before the allocated buffer.
cves.impact:
summary: The out-of-bounds write can cause a memory corruption which can have various consequences including a Denial of Service. The OPENSSL_uni2utf8() function performs a two-pass conversion of a PKCS#12 BMPString (UTF-16BE) to UTF-8. In the second pass, when emitting UTF-8 bytes, the helper function bmp_to_utf8() incorrectly forwards the remaining UTF-16 source byte count as the destination buffer capacity to UTF8_putc(). For BMP code points above U+07FF, UTF-8 requires three bytes, but the forwarded capacity can be just two bytes. UTF8_putc() then returns -1, and this negative value is added to the output length without validation, causing the length to become negative. The subsequent trailing NUL byte is then written at a negative offset, causing write outside of heap allocated buffer. The vulnerability is reachable via the public PKCS12_get_friendlyname() API when parsing attacker-controlled PKCS#12 files. While PKCS12_parse() uses a different code path that avoids this issue, PKCS12_get_friendlyname() directly invokes the vulnerable function. Exploitation requires an attacker to provide a malicious PKCS#12 file to be parsed by the application and the attacker can just trigger a one zero byte write before the allocated buffer. For that reason the issue was assessed as Low severity according to our Security Policy. The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue, as the PKCS#12 implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary. OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3, 3.0 and 1.1.1 are vulnerable to this issue. OpenSSL 1.0.2 is not affected by this issue. (CVE-2025-69419)

cves.description: Issue summary: A type confusion vulnerability exists in the TimeStamp Response verification code where an ASN1_TYPE union member is accessed without first validating the type, causing an invalid or NULL pointer dereference when processing a malformed TimeStamp Response file.
cves.impact:
summary: An application calling TS_RESP_verify_response() with a malformed TimeStamp Response can be caused to dereference an invalid or NULL pointer when reading, resulting in a Denial of Service. The functions ossl_ess_get_signing_cert() and ossl_ess_get_signing_cert_v2() access the signing cert attribute value without validating its type. Exploiting this vulnerability requires an attacker to provide a malformed TimeStamp Response to an application that verifies timestamp responses. The TimeStamp protocol (RFC 3161) is not widely used and the impact of the exploit is just a Denial of Service. For these reasons the issue was assessed as Low severity. The FIPS modules in 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue, as the TimeStamp Response implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary. cves.description: CVE-2025-71066 In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net/sched: ets: Always remove class from active list before deleting in ets_qdisc_change zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com says: The vulnerability is a race condition between `ets_qdisc_dequeue` and `ets_qdisc_change`. It leads to UAF on `struct Qdisc` object. Attacker requires the capability to create new user and network namespace in order to trigger the bug. See my additional commentary at the end of the analysis. Analysis: static int ets_qdisc_change(struct Qdisc *sch, struct nlattr *opt, struct netlink_ext_ack *extack) { ... // (1) this lock is preventing .change handler (`ets_qdisc_change`) //to race with .dequeue handler (`ets_qdisc_dequeue`) sch_tree_lock(sch); for (i = nbands; i < oldbands; i++) { if (i >= q->nstrict && q->classes[i].qdisc->q.qlen) list_del_init(&q->classes[i].alist); qdisc_purge_queue(q->classes[i].qdisc); } WRITE_ONCE(q->nbands, nbands); for (i = nstrict; i < q->nstrict; i++) { if (q->classes[i].qdisc->q.qlen) { // (2) the class is added to the q->active list_add_tail(&q->classes[i].alist, &q->active); q->classes[i].deficit = quanta[i]; } } WRITE_ONCE(q->nstrict, nstrict); memcpy(q->prio2band, priomap, sizeof(priomap)); for (i = 0; i < q->nbands; i++) WRITE_ONCE(q->classes[i].quantum, quanta[i]); for (i = oldbands; i < q->nbands; i++) { q->classes[i].qdisc = queues[i]; if (q->classes[i].qdisc != &noop_qdisc) qdisc_hash_add(q->classes[i].qdisc, true); } // (3) the qdisc is unlocked, now dequeue can be called in parallel // to the rest of .change handler sch_tree_unlock(sch); ets_offload_change(sch); for (i = q->nbands; i < oldbands; i++) { // (4) we're reducing the refcount for our class's qdisc and // freeing it qdisc_put(q->classes[i].qdisc); // (5) If we call .dequeue between (4) and (5), we will have // a strong UAF and we can control RIP q->classes[i].qdisc = NULL; WRITE_ONCE(q->classes[i].quantum, 0); q->classes[i].deficit = 0; gnet_stats_basic_sync_init(&q->classes[i].bstats); memset(&q->classes[i].qstats, 0, sizeof(q->classes[i].qstats)); } return 0; } Comment: This happens because some of the classes have their qdiscs assigned to NULL, but remain in the active list. This commit fixes this issue by always removing the class from the active list before deleting and freeing its associated qdisc Reproducer Steps (trimmed version of what was sent by zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com) ``` DEV="${DEV:-lo}" ROOT_HANDLE="${ROOT_HANDLE:-1:}" BAND2_HANDLE="${BAND2_HANDLE:-20:}" # child under 1:2 PING_BYTES="${PING_BYTES:-48}" PING_COUNT="${PING_COUNT:-200000}" PING_DST="${PING_DST:-127.0.0.1}" SLOW_TBF_RATE="${SLOW_TBF_RATE:-8bit}" SLOW_TBF_BURST="${SLOW_TBF_BURST:-100b}" SLOW_TBF_LAT="${SLOW_TBF_LAT:-1s}" cleanup() { tc qdisc del dev "$DEV" root 2>/dev/null } trap cleanup EXIT ip link set "$DEV" up tc qdisc del dev "$DEV" root 2>/dev/null || true tc qdisc add dev "$DEV" root handle "$ROOT_HANDLE" ets bands 2 strict 2 tc qdisc add dev "$DEV" parent 1:2 handle "$BAND2_HANDLE" \ tbf rate "$SLOW_TBF_RATE" burst "$SLOW_TBF_BURST" latency "$SLOW_TBF_LAT" tc filter add dev "$DEV" parent 1: protocol all prio 1 u32 match u32 0 0 flowid 1:2 tc -s qdisc ls dev $DEV ping -I "$DEV" -f -c "$PING_COUNT" -s "$PING_BYTES" -W 0.001 "$PING_DST" \ >/dev/null 2>&1 & tc qdisc change dev "$DEV" root handle "$ROOT_HANDLE" ets bands 2 strict 0 tc qdisc change dev "$DEV" root handle "$ROOT_HANDLE" ets bands 2 strict 2 tc -s qdisc ls dev $DEV tc qdisc del dev "$DEV" parent ---truncated---

cves.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: net: stmmac: fix the crash issue for zero copy XDP_TX action There is a crash issue when running zero copy XDP_TX action, the crash log is shown below. [ 216.122464] Unable to handle kernel paging request at virtual address fffeffff80000000 [ 216.187524] Internal error: Oops: 0000000096000144 [#1] SMP [ 216.301694] Call trace: [ 216.304130] dcache_clean_poc+0x20/0x38 (P) [ 216.308308] __dma_sync_single_for_device+0x1bc/0x1e0 [ 216.313351] stmmac_xdp_xmit_xdpf+0x354/0x400 [ 216.317701] __stmmac_xdp_run_prog+0x164/0x368 [ 216.322139] stmmac_napi_poll_rxtx+0xba8/0xf00 [ 216.326576] __napi_poll+0x40/0x218 [ 216.408054] Kernel panic - not syncing: Oops: Fatal exception in interrupt For XDP_TX action, the xdp_buff is converted to xdp_frame by xdp_convert_buff_to_frame(). The memory type of the resulting xdp_frame depends on the memory type of the xdp_buff. For page pool based xdp_buff it produces xdp_frame with memory type MEM_TYPE_PAGE_POOL. For zero copy XSK pool based xdp_buff it produces xdp_frame with memory type MEM_TYPE_PAGE_ORDER0. However, stmmac_xdp_xmit_back() does not check the memory type and always uses the page pool type, this leads to invalid mappings and causes the crash. Therefore, check the xdp_buff memory type in stmmac_xdp_xmit_back() to fix this issue. (CVE-2025-71095)

cves.impact:
A remote unauthenticated attacker can trigger excessive resource consumption to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the vulnerable system.

The following BIG-IP DNS configuration is not affected by this vulnerability:

Listener (virtual server) with Use BIND Server on BIG-IP setting disabled on the attached DNS profile.

The following BIG-IP DNS configuration is not affected by this vulnerability:

Listener (virtual server) with Use BIND Server on BIG-IP setting enabled on the attached DNS profile. However, the named configuration must include recursion no.
cves.mitigation:
BIG-IP DNS

To mitigate this vulnerability, you can either disable BIND in the DNS profile if it's not required, or ensure that recursion is set to no in the named configuration. To do so, perform one of the following procedures:

Disabling the Use BIND Server on BIG-IP option in the DNS profile
Change the recursion line to no in the named configuration file (recursion is set to no by default)

Disabling the Use BIND Server on BIG-IP option in the DNS profile

Impact of action: Disabling the BIND server can affect DNS configurations that use BIND as a fallback method (return to DNS) for resolution.

Log in to the Configuration utility.
Go to Local Traffic > Profiles > Services > DNS.
Select the applicable DNS profile.
For the Use BIND Server on BIG-IP option, select Disabled.
Select Finished.

Change the recursion line to no in the named configuration file (recursion is set to no by default)

Log in to the Configuration utility.
Go to DNS > Zones > ZoneRunner > named Configuration.
In the Options box, scroll down to the options section.
Find the recursion yes; statement and replace it with recursion no;.
Select Update.

cves.description: CVE-2025-8713 PostgreSQL optimizer statistics allow a user to read sampled data within a view that the user cannot access. Separately, statistics allow a user to read sampled data that a row security policy intended to hide. PostgreSQL maintains statistics for tables by sampling data available in columns; this data is consulted during the query planning process. Prior to this release, a user could craft a leaky operator that bypassed view access control lists (ACLs) and bypassed row security policies in partitioning or table inheritance hierarchies. Reachable statistics data notably included histograms and most-common-values lists. CVE-2017-7484 and CVE-2019-10130 intended to close this class of vulnerability, but this gap remained. Versions before PostgreSQL 17.6, 16.10, 15.14, 14.19, and 13.22 are affected.

cves.description: A flaw was found in linux-pam. The pam_namespace module may improperly handle user-controlled paths, allowing local users to exploit symlink attacks and race conditions to elevate their privileges to root. This CVE provides a "complete" fix for CVE-2025-6020. (CVE-2025-8941)
cves.impact: This vulnerability in pam_namespace is rated important because it allows a local, unprivileged user to escalate privileges to root by exploiting symlink attacks or race conditions in polyinstantiated directories under their control. Successful exploitation requires only the ability to create and manipulate filesystem paths in such directories, without the need for special capabilities or kernel-level vulnerabilities. In multi-user environments—such as shared systems, terminal servers, or certain container deployments—an unprotected or misconfigured pam_namespace configuration can serve as a single point of compromise. Privilege escalation flaws of this nature may also be chained with other vulnerabilities to maintain persistence or evade detection, further increasing the overall impact.
cves.mitigation: To mitigate this vulnerability, you should permit management access to F5 products only over a secure network and restrict command line/Configuration utility access for affected systems to only administrative users.

cves.description: 1. A cookie is set using the `secure` keyword for `https://target` 2. curl is redirected to or otherwise made to speak with `http://target` (same hostname, but using clear text HTTP) using the same cookie set 3. The same cookie name is set - but with just a slash as path (`path='/'`). Since this site is not secure, the cookie *should* just be ignored. 4. A bug in the path comparison logic makes curl read outside a heap buffer boundary The bug either causes a crash or it potentially makes the comparison come to the wrong conclusion and lets the clear-text site override the contents of the secure cookie, contrary to expectations and depending on the memory contents immediately following the single-byte allocation that holds the path. The presumed and correct behavior would be to plainly ignore the second set of the cookie since it was already set as secure on a secure host so overriding it on an insecure host should not be okay. (CVE-2025-9086)

cves.description: Passing too large an alignment to the memalign suite of functions (memalign, posix_memalign, aligned_alloc) in the GNU C Library version 2.30 to 2.42 may result in an integer overflow, which could consequently result in a heap corruption. Note that the attacker must have control over both, the size as well as the alignment arguments of the memalign function to be able to exploit this. The size parameter must be close enough to PTRDIFF_MAX so as to overflow size_t along with the large alignment argument. This limits the malicious inputs for the alignment for memalign to the range [1<<62+ 1, 1<<63] and exactly 1<<63 for posix_memalign and aligned_alloc. Typically the alignment argument passed to such functions is a known constrained quantity (e.g. page size, block size, struct sizes) and is not attacker controlled, because of which this may not be easily exploitable in practice. An application bug could potentially result in the input alignment being too large, e.g. due to a different buffer overflow or integer overflow in the application or its dependent libraries, but that is again an uncommon usage pattern given typical sources of alignments. (CVE-2026-0861)

cves.description: NGINX JavaScript (njs) has a vulnerability where the njs XML module exposes entity-backed XML attributes inconsistently with libxml2 canonicalization. In both the built-in njs and QuickJS backends during the canonicalization process, the $attr$Name getter may return undefined for an explicitly present attribute containing an internal entity reference. The $attrs getter may return a value derived only from the first attribute child. This may allow an unauthenticated attacker that invests significant effort in obtaining a genuinely signed document to skip validation while signature verification succeeds. An nginx-saml deployment is a confirmed affected consumer when run with the built-in njs backend. (CVE-2026-101019)
cves.impact: In affected signed-XML consumers, an unauthenticated attacker can cause security-relevant attributes to appear absent or truncated while signature verification succeeds. In nginx-saml deployments, this issue can enable the attacker to bypass expiry, Destination, and request-correlation checks, enabling replay or acceptance of a response outside its intended context. Exploitation does not permit signature or identity forgery and does not impact availability.
cves.mitigation:
Applications processing signed XML should reject DTD-bearing input before calling xml.parse(). The check must cover the complete document after decoding its accepted input encoding; a parser-level DTD prohibition is preferable to a raw byte search for "<!DOCTYPE". Applications should also treat absent security-relevant attributes as validation failures rather than optional values. An nginx-saml deployment should explicitly validate Destination; request correlation when unsolicited SSO is not intended; and request assertion validity, bearer SubjectConfirmation, Recipient, and SubjectConfirmationData InResponseTo checks.

Acknowledgments

This issue was discovered internally by F5.

cves.description: NGINX JavaScript (njs) has a vulnerability where the built-in njs engine leaks a libxml2 parser context when xml.parse() fails. The failure path did not register cleanup and the context was not released for the lifetime of the process. An unauthenticated attacker may send requests with malformed XML and can cause unbounded memory growth in long-lived NGINX worker processes. (CVE-2026-101025)
cves.impact: This vulnerability may allow remote attackers to send requests that trigger repeated parsing of malformed XML and may lead to NGINX worker termination or denial-of-service (DoS). There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
Use the QuickJS (qjs) engine with js_engine qjs;, which is not affected. Where migration is not possible, avoid passing attacker-controlled XML to xml.parse(), reject, or rate-limit malformed input, and use worker memory limits.

Acknowledgments

This issue was discovered internally by F5.

cves.description: CVE-2026-104711 Improper neutralization of special elements used in an expression language statement ('Expression Language Injection') vulnerability in Apache Struts. If the application is configured to use the legacy RESTful action mapper, a crafted request can inject an OGNL expression that may lead to remote code execution. Struts 7 is affected only when the OGNL allowlist is disabled; it is enabled by default. Applications using the default action mapper, the restful2 mapper, or the Struts REST plugin are not affected. This issue affects Apache Struts: from 2.0.0 through 2.3.37, from 2.5.0 through 2.5.33, from 6.0.0 through 6.11.0, from 7.0.0 through 7.3.0. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 6.12.0 or 7.4.0, which fixes the issue.

This issue affects Apache Struts: from 2.5.14 through 2.5.33, from 6.0.0 through 6.11.0, from 7.0.0 through 7.3.0. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 6.12.0 or 7.4.0, which fixes the issue.

Specific mitigation procedure for Next.js Image Optimizer RCE for node.js CVE-2026-111497
Create a custom attack signature for node.js CVE-2026-111497
Specific mitigation procedure for Next.js Image Optimizer RCE for node.js CVE-2026-111497

This procedure is relevant for Next.js apps hosted on vulnerable Node.js servers. F5 recommends to restrict the list of domains in the`url`parameter under the allowed URL `/_next/image` to include only trusted websites.

Configure an allowed URL named "/_next/image"

As an Administrator role user, navigate to Security ›› Application Security : URLs : Allowed URLs : Allowed HTTP URLs
Select the specific Adv WAF security policy
Click Create
Under Create New Allowed URL, set Explicit, HTTPS, '/_next/image'
Remove Perform Staging to immediately enforce the URL
Click Create
The created HTTPS /_next/image URL is now listed in the Allowed URL list.

Configure a URL parameter named "url"

Click on the HTTPS /_next/image URL in the Allowed URL list, it will open the page
Security ›› Application Security : URLs : Allowed URLs : Allowed HTTP URLs ›› Allowed HTTP URL Properties
Click on URL Parameters, it will open the page
Security ›› Application Security : URLs : Allowed URLs : Allowed HTTP URLs ›› URL Parameters
Click Create, it will open the page
Security ›› Application Security : URLs : Allowed URLs : Allowed HTTP URLs ›› Add URL Parameter…
Set Parameter Name as Explicit 'url'
Set Parameter Level as URL, Path HTTPS '/_next/image'
Uncheck Perform Staging to immediately enforce the URL parameter
Set Parameter Value Type to 'User input value'

The ’url’ Parameter’s Data Type can be configured with two options. Each option will use a different Adv WAF policy violation.

Option 1:

Set the 'Data Type' as 'URI' and the 'Host Name Representation' as 'Domain Name'
Under Data Type, Set the 'Data Type' as 'URI' and the 'Host Name Representation' as 'Domain Name'
Click Create
The newly created URL Parameter 'url' will be listed in the URL Parameters List

Configure Learn, Alarm and Block settings on 'Illegal Parameter Data Type' Violation on Specific Adv WAF Security Policy

Navigate to Security ›› Application Security : Policy Building : Learning and Blocking Settings
Select the specific Adv WAF security policy
Under Parameters, Enable Alarm and Block settings on 'Illegal Parameter Data Type' violation
Click Save

Configure disallowed host names or IP addresses under SSRF Protection

Illegal Parameter Data Type violation works in tandem with the Adv WAF security policy's SSRF protection configuration.

Navigate to Security ›› Application Security : Security Policies : Policies List > select the specific Adv WAF security policy
Under Advanced Protection, SSRF Protection, add in the list the specific hosts that you want to disallow access to. You can use either IP addresses or host names in each entry.
Note: under URI Data Type Parameters to Mitigate SSRF Evasions, it should list the ‘url’ parameter
Click Save

Note: When configuring host names or domain names under SSRF Protection, ensure these can be resolved by the DNS server configured in the BIG-IP Adv WAF system.

 

Option 2:

Set the 'Data Type' as 'Alpha-Numeric' and define allowed specific pattern for the 'url' parameter value
Under Data Type, Set the 'Data Type' as 'Alpha-Numeric'
Under Regular Expression box, set the regular expression of the allowed specific pattern
For example:

http://site\.trusted\.local(?:/[^\s]*)?
Click Create
The newly created URL Parameter 'url' will be listed in the URL Parameters List

Configure Alarm and Block settings on ‘Parameter value does not comply with regular expression' Violation on Specific Adv WAF Security Policy

Navigate to Security ›› Application Security : Policy Building : Learning and Blocking Settings
Select the specific Adv WAF security policy
Under Parameters, Enable Alarm and Block settings on ' Parameter value does not comply with regular expression' violation
Click Save

Configure Trusted Website Domains

Navigate to Security ›› Application Security : Security Policies : Policies List, Click on the specific Adv WAF Security Policy
Under the Policy configuration page , HTTP Message Protection, Select Headers
Under Host Names, depending on your needs, select Include or Exclude Subdomains, then set the 'Host Name' of the Trusted Website Domains
Example:
If Include Subdomains selected, '(and Sub-Domains' is listed: images.trusted.net (and Sub-Domains)
If Exclude Subdomains selected, specific hostname is listed: secure.trusted.net

Configure Alarm and Block settings on ‘Illegal host name' violation on Specific Adv WAF Security Policy

Navigate to Security ›› Application Security : Policy Building : Learning and Blocking Settings
Select the specific Adv WAF security policy
Under Parameters, Enable Alarm and Block settings on ' Illegal host name' violation
Click Save
Click Apply Policy (at the top right corner)
Create a custom attack signature for node.js CVE-2026-111497
As an administrator role user, navigate to Security ›› Options : Application Security : Attack Signatures > Attack Signatures List
Click Create
Provide an Attack Signature Name, example temp_nodejsCVE-2026-111497
Assign a Tag, example temp_nodejsCVE-2026-111497:
For Signature Type, use Request
For Attack Type, use Command Execution
For Assigned Systems, use Node.js
For Rule, use Advanced Mode. Paste the custom rule:

headercontent:"Content-Encoding:"; nocase; re2:"/^Content-Encoding:[^\n]+\bbr\b/Hmi"; re2:"/^(?:POST|PUT|PATCH)/i";

Note: This signature blocks all requests with an "Content-Encoding" header that indicates the Brotli compression method, while limiting to POST/PUT/PATCH method to reduce false positives.
Set Accuracy, example Low
Set Risk, example Low
Click Add

Create a custom attack signature set and configure to match the custom attack signature

Navigate to Security ›› Options : Application Security : Attack Signatures > Attack Signatures Sets
Click Create
Provide an Attack Signature Set Name, example temp_nodejsCVE-2026-111497
Set Default Blocking Actions, example Learn, Alarm, Block
Set 'Assign Set to Newly Created Policies', example Always
Set 'Signature Set Type' , example Manual, then use one of the available filters, example Tag, and use the custom attack signatures Tag, example temp_nodejsCVE-2026-111497. The matched attack signature will appear in the Available Signatures list. Click on the plus sign to assign the Attack Signature.
Click Add
The newly created Attack Signature set will appear in the list.

Assign the Custom Attack Signature Set to the specific Adv WAF Security Policy

Navigate to Security ›› Application Security : Policy Building : Learning and Blocking Settings
In the dropdown list, select the specific Adv WAF Security Policy
Under Attack Signatures, click Change
Click the checkbox next to the newly created Custom Attack Signature Set, then click Change
Enable the Attack Signature Set's violation settings, example enable Learn, Alarm, Block checkboxes
Click on Save

Ensure that the newly created custom attack signature is Enforced

Navigate to Security ›› Application Security : Security Policies : Policies List > select the specific Adv WAF Security Policy
Under Policy Configuration, Attack Signatures, select the custom attack signature, click Enforce
Click Apply Policy

cves.title: K000163710: BIND vulnerability CVE-2026-10723

cves.description: If BIND encounters a particular invalid data structure in a DNS record, it will accept the invalid data, and may subsequently abort and exit. BIND will first need to store a DNS record for a key (KEY, DNSKEY, etc.). That key must specify a PRIVATEDNS algorithm (253), and in the algorithm identifier, improperly give a length longer than the actual identifier data. The invalid identifier will be stored. If BIND later needs to render that record to text, it will use the invalid length during processing, leading to a consistency check failing. This issue affects BIND 9 versions 9.18.0 through 9.18.50, 9.20.0 through 9.20.24, 9.21.0 through 9.21.23, 9.18.11-S1 through 9.18.50-S1, and 9.20.9-S1 through 9.20.24-S1. (CVE-2026-10822)
cves.impact: This vulnerability allows a denial-of-service (DoS) when BIND processes a DNS KEY/DNSKEY record specifying a PRIVATEDNS algorithm (253) where the algorithm identifier length field is larger than the actual identifier data. BIND accepts and stores the invalid record without validation. When BIND later attempts to render that record to text, it uses the incorrect length, causing an internal consistency check to fail and the named process to abort. When the BIG-IP DNS is configured as a recursive resolver with BIND enabled and DNS cache enabled, an attacker controlling or spoofing an authoritative zone can serve a malformed PRIVATEDNS algorithm-253 DNSKEY record, causing the named process to crash and resulting in a DoS.

To mitigate this issue, you can disable BIND, disable DNS caching, or disable recursion.

Disable the Use BIND Server on BIG-IP option in the DNS profile
Disable DNS caching in the DNS profile
⁠Restrict DNS recursion on the BIG-IP DNS system

Disable the Use BIND Server on BIG-IP option in the DNS profile

Important: Disabling the BIND server can affect DNS configurations that use BIND as a fallback method (return to DNS) for resolution.

Log in to the Configuration utility.
Go to one of the following locations:
Local Traffic > Profiles > Services > DNS.
DNS > Delivery > Profiles > DNS.
Select the applicable DNS profile.
For Use BIND Server on BIG-IP, select Disabled.
Select Update.

Disable DNS caching in the DNS profile

Impact of procedure: Caching allows the BIG-IP system to answer repeated queries from memory. With caching disabled, every query must be sent to external nameservers, local DNS server pools, or processed by the local BIND instance, introducing network and processing latency. Additionally, clearing the DNS cache will require the cache to be rebuilt if the cache is re-enabled, resulting in a temporary rise in resolution latency. F5 recommends that you evaluate changes in your test environment prior to making changes to the production environment.

Log in to the Configuration utility.
Go to one of the following locations:
Local Traffic > Profiles > Services > DNS.
DNS > Delivery > Profiles > DNS.
Select the applicable DNS profile.
In the DNS Features section, locate DNS Cache and select Disabled from the list.
Select Update.
Go to DNS > Caches > Statistics.
Select the check box next to the cache you want to clear.
Select Clear Cache.

cves.description:
CVE-2026-109618 (also known as php2shell)

PHP uses longjmp() for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE).
cves.impact:
APM Data Plane
This vulnerability may allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary system commands, create or delete files, or disable services.
Control Plane
This vulnerability may allow a remote authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary system commands, create or delete files, or disable services.
cves.mitigation:
BIG-IP mitigation
BIG-IP Configuration utility mitigation
Protection for your backend pool members
BIG-IP mitigation

The following mitigates BIG-IP control plane configuration utility exposure as well as BIG-IP APM data plane exposure.

At a high level, the admin needs to login on BIG-IP with advanced shell, create a new file with the content below, and restart apache.

Important: F5 recommends that you verify the following php.ini configuration in your testing/staging environment before deploying to your production environment.

Note: If you have a multi bladed system these steps must be done on each individual blade.

Create a new file - /etc/php.ini.d/K000163821.ini and include the content below.

; The configuration mitigations recommended by PHP for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 
; These will NOT survive an upgrade of BIG-IP TMOS. 
memory_limit = -1 
post_max_size = 8M 
upload_max_filesize = 7M 
session.upload_progress.enabled = 0

Restart apache using bigstart restart httpd.

On multi-bladed systems, restart apache using clsh bigstart restart httpd.

Only for BIG-IP APM systems, restart apache using bigstart restart httpd_sam.

On multi-bladed BIG-IP APM systems, restart apache using clsh bigstart restart httpd_sam.

Note: Restarting the httpd_sam process may disrupt webtop connections, requiring users to reconnect.

If you have configured a device group, repeat on each high availability (HA) peer in the group.
BIG-IP Configuration utility mitigation

In addition to the above mitigation, you can also restrict access to the Configuration utility (the control plane) using the following procedures:

Block Configuration utility access through self IP addresses
Block Configuration utility access through the management interface
Block Configuration utility access through self IP addresses

You can block all access to the Configuration utility of your BIG-IP system using self IP addresses. To do so, you can change the Port Lockdown setting to Allow None for each self IP address on the system. If you must open any ports, you should use the Allow Custom option, taking care to block access to the Configuration utility. By default, the Configuration utility listens on TCP port 443. If you modified the default port, ensure that you block access to the alternate port you configured.

Note: Performing this action prevents all access to the Configuration utility and iControl REST using the self IP address. These changes may also impact other services, including breaking high availability (HA) configurations. For more information, refer to K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules.

Before you make changes to the configuration of your self IP addresses, F5 strongly recommends that you refer to the following articles:

K17333: Overview of port lockdown behavior (12.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K31003634: The Configuration utility of the Single-NIC BIG-IP Virtual Edition now defaults to TCP port 8443
K51358480: The single-NIC BIG-IP VE may erroneously revert to the default management httpd port after a configuration reload

If you must expose port 443 on your self IP addresses and want to restrict access to specific IP ranges, you may consider using the packet filtering functionality built into the BIG-IP system. For more information, refer to the following article:

K13383: Configure CIDR Network Addresses for the BIG-IP packet filter
Block Configuration utility access through the management interface

To mitigate this vulnerability for affected F5 products, you should restrict management access to F5 products to only trusted users and devices over a secure network. For more information about securing access to BIG-IP systems, refer to the following articles:

K13309: Restricting access to the Configuration utility by source IP address (11.x - 17.x)
K13092: Overview of securing access to the BIG-IP system
K46122561: Restrict access to the BIG-IP management interface using network firewall rules
Protection for your backend pool members

The following will mitigate the exposure of backend applications.

If you are using BIG-IP Advanced WAF, BIG-IP ASM, F5 WAF for NGINX, F5 WAF for Distributed Cloud (https://www.f5cloudstatus.com/incidents/r7t009rtmd3k) or NGINX App Protect WAF to protect your backend pool members, you can mitigate this vulnerability for your backend pool members by using the following attack signatures enabled in blocking mode:

CVE-2026-109618: PHP Remote Code Execution, ID 200103697 and ID 200204115
200103697 - ASM/Adv WAF Attack Signature Sets: WebSphere signatures, Server Side Code Injection Signatures, Low and Medium Accuracy Signatures, All Signatures
200204115 - ASM/Adv WAF Attack Signature Sets: WebSphere signatures, Server Side Code Injection Signatures, Low and Medium Accuracy Signatures, All Signatures
CVE-2026-109619: PHP Remote Code Execution, ID 200204113
200204113 - ASM/Adv WAF Attack Signature Sets: WebSphere signatures, Server Side Code Injection Signatures, Low and Medium Accuracy Signatures, All Signatures

These attack signatures are part of the newly released attack signature update ASM-AttackSignatures_20261022_154742.im; you must perform a signature file update to ASM-AttackSignatures_20261022_154742.im or later for these signatures to be available on your system.

For information about updating attack signatures on the BIG-IP system, refer to K82512024: Managing BIG-IP ASM Live Updates. For information about assigning attack signatures to security policies on the BIG-IP system, refer to the Assigning Attack Signatures to Security Policies chapter of the BIG-IP Application Security Manager: Attack and Bot Signatures guide.

For information about updating attack signatures on the NGINX system, refer to the Update F5 WAF for NGINX signatures chapter of the F5 WAF for NGINX guide.

For information about updating attack signatures on the F5 Distributed Cloud instance, refer to Best Practices for Signature Staging guide for F5 WAF for Distributed Cloud.

Additionally, you can use the BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM system to mitigate the impact of the php2shell vulnerabilities in your infrastructure using the following procedures:

PHP RCE from out-of-memory (OOM) corruption - CVE-2026-109618
Mitigation Configuration on BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM for CVE-2026-109619

Important: The following BIG-IP controls reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not replace patching.

PHP RCE from out-of-memory (OOM) corruption - CVE-2026-109618
Before configuring the BIG-IP system
Identify all ASM policies protecting the affected PHP applications.
Save backups of all identified policies.
Review legitimate upload, form, and API requirements before introducing restrictions.
Recommended BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM configuration
Block unnecessary multipart requests

For applications that do not require multipart submissions:

Open the relevant security policy’s Allowed URLs configuration.
In Header-Based Content Profiles, add or modify an entry matching the Content-Type header for *multipart*.
Set the action to Disallow.
Enable Alarm and Block for Illegal request content type.
Apply the restriction to all relevant URL entries (explicit and wildcards).

This prevents blocked requests from reaching PHP’s multipart parser. It will also prevent legitimate multipart uploads and forms.

Limit request size

In the policy’s File Types configuration:

Enable POST Data Length checking and set the smallest maximum body size the application requires.
Enable Request Length checking and set an appropriate total-request limit, allowing for headers and the URL.
Review explicit file types, the wildcard entry, and the no-extension entry.
Enable Alarm and Block for Illegal POST data length and Illegal request length.

PHP recommends a conservative backend post_max_size: 8M where uploads are unnecessary or 32M where uploads are required. These are exposure-reduction guidelines, not guaranteed safe WAF thresholds. The WAF max request buffer size is by default 10M so the recommendation is to limit to 8M.

Limit input complexity and enforce protocol checks

Under HTTP Protocol Compliance, enable:

Check maximum number of parameters — reduce the maximum to the application’s required count.
Check maximum number of headers — set an application-appropriate maximum.
Bad multipart/form-data request parsing.
Bad multipart parameters parsing.
Unparsable request content.
Several Content-Length headers.
Chunked request with Content-Length header.

Enable Alarm and Block for HTTP protocol compliance failed. Also configure an appropriate HTTP header-length limit and block Illegal header length. Where practical, allow only expected form parameters. If array-style parameter names are unnecessary, restrict, and in parameter names and block Illegal meta character in parameter name.

Important: Small, valid multipart requests can still cause excessive PHP memory allocation. Ordinary HTTP header limits do not establish a limit on headers inside multipart parts, and parameter-count checks must not be assumed to count every empty file control. These controls do not fully address all documented OOM techniques.

Require a declared length for POST requests

Where application compatibility permits, reject POST requests without a valid Content-Length header. This reduces exposure to the documented attack path in which PHP processes multipart data without a usable declared length.

Under HTTP Protocol Compliance, enable POST request with Content-Length: 0.
Enable Alarm and Block for HTTP protocol compliance failed, then apply the policy.
Separately enforce the presence of Content-Length on POST requests using a method-scoped BIG-IP local traffic policy or iRule. The POST request with Content-Length: 0 check should not be treated as a general missing-header check.
Continue enforcing actual request-body size limits and rejecting ambiguous framing, including requests containing both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length.

Compatibility impact: Requiring Content-Length rejects otherwise valid chunked POST requests and HTTP/2 POST requests that omit it. Blocking zero-length POST requests can also disrupt legitimate application workflows.

Limitation: A valid Content-Length does not prevent memory amplification or other OOM triggers. These restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace updating PHP.

Apply the policy and validate
Set the policy to Blocking, resolve relevant staging or bypass exceptions, and Apply Policy.
Confirm prohibited and over-limit requests are blocked before reaching PHP.
Test legitimate uploads, forms and APIs, and monitor WAF events and application availability.
Prevent direct-origin access that bypasses the BIG-IP system.
Complete the PHP update promptly, then review temporary restrictions.
Mitigation Configuration on BIG-IP Advanced WAF/ASM for CVE-2026-109619
Block the PHP session upload-progress parameter (Where PHP session upload progress is not required)

Under Security --> Application Security --> Parameters --> Parameter List:

Create an Explicit parameter named PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, or the name configured in PHP’s session.upload_progress.name.
Set its value type to User Input and data type to Alpha-Numeric.
Enable regular-expression validation with an expression that rejects every value. (?!) is a candidate deny-all PCRE expression; confirm that the deployed BIG-IP version accepts and enforces it.
Disable Allow Empty Value so an empty value cannot bypass validation.
Leave Mandatory disabled—requests without this parameter should remain allowed.
Disable staging for this parameter.

Under Security --> Application Security --> Policy Building --> Learning and Blocking Settings:

Enable Alarm and Block in the Parameters section for:

Parameter value does not comply with regular expression
Illegal empty parameter value

Ensure the policy is in Blocking mode and Apply Policy.

Review URL-specific definitions that could override a global parameter definition. Ensure multipart bodies are parsed as Form Data.

Validate: Requests containing the parameter, with either empty or non-empty values, must be blocked. Requests without it should continue working, including those permitted by existing wildcards.

PHP has various global state that temporarily points into request memory. In some scenarios, global state may not be correctly reset, or may be repopulated after being reset. The global state may then refer to request memory even after it has been freed. Subsequent requests may read or branch on this stale state before it is fully initialized. Multiple strategies can trigger this condition and produce remote code execution (RCE).

The ’url’ Parameter’s Data Type can be configured with two options. Each option will use a different Adv WAF policy violation.

Set the 'Data Type' as 'URI' and the 'Host Name Representation' as 'Domain Name'
Under Data Type, Set the 'Data Type' as 'URI' and the 'Host Name Representation' as 'Domain Name'

Assign a Tag, example temp_nodejsCVE-2026-111497:

cves.description: X.509 trust-chain bypass in the OpenSSL compatibility certificate verifier (wolfSSL_X509_verify_cert()). This affects only builds with --enable-opensslextra (OPENSSL_EXTRA) and whose application validates certificates by calling X509_verify_cert() with caller-supplied untrusted intermediate certificates; for those users it is critical, otherwise the library is unaffected. In particular, native wolfSSL TLS/DTLS usage is not impacted. wolfSSL's X509_verify_cert() temporarily loads each caller-supplied untrusted intermediate into the certificate manager but failed to drop them before the trusted-store check, so an untrusted intermediate could anchor the path itself. An attacker can present a chain that never reaches a configured trust anchor and have it accepted, resulting in acceptance of an attacker-controlled certificate. This is certificate verification independent of TLS (e.g. S/MIME/CMS, code/firmware signing, JWT/JWS x5c), is not specific to any key type or algorithm, and a single untrusted intermediate suffices. The default wolfSSL TLS handshake (WOLFSSL_VERIFY_PEER) is not affected; only TLS applications doing manual or deferred peer verification through this API are, which also requires --enable-sessioncerts. (CVE-2026-11310)

cves.description: When NGINX Plus is configured as the data plane for NGINX Gateway Fabric, an injection vulnerability exists in the NGINX configuration generator component of NGINX Gateway Fabric. User-supplied string values from the NginxProxy Custom Resource Definition serverTokens field and the AuthenticationFilter Custom Resource Definition extraAuthArgs field are rendered directly into NGINX configuration templates without sanitization or escaping. An authenticated attacker with permission to create or modify these Custom Resource Definitions may craft values that inject arbitrary NGINX configuration directives. This is a control plane issue; there is no data plane exposure from the vulnerability trigger itself. (CVE-2026-11311)
cves.impact: An authenticated attacker granted write access to the NginxProxy or AuthenticationFilter Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) on a Kubernetes cluster running NGINX Gateway Fabric with NGINX Plus may inject arbitrary NGINX http-context directives, including rogue server blocks. Successful exploitation may allow the attacker to expose sensitive data from the NGINX pod filesystem, proxy traffic to attacker-controlled endpoints, or cause a denial-of-service (DoS) condition by injecting configuration that prevents NGINX from reloading. This issue affects NGINX Gateway Fabric with NGINX Plus only; NGINX Open Source deployments are not affected. There is no data plane exposure; this is a control plane issue only.
cves.mitigation:
As this attack is conducted by authenticated users with Kubernetes role-based access control (RBAC) write access to the affected CRDs, the only complete mitigation is to restrict that access to fully trusted administrators only. F5 recommends the following mitigation strategy:

Restrict write access to the NginxProxy and AuthenticationFilter CRDs to trusted cluster administrators only, using Kubernetes RBAC.
Do not configure custom serverTokens values; leave it unset (the default value is off) or use only the permitted keywords: off, on, build.
Do not configure extraAuthArgs values. If you have already configured extraAuthArgs values, check the values for special characters and remove them. For example, semi-colon (;), number sign (#), and quotation marks ("").

Acknowledgments

This issue was discovered internally by F5.

cves.description: An attacker who knows (or guesses) that a resolver uses RPZ with wildcard CNAME policies can craft query names long enough to trigger a NAMETOOLONG error condition during RPZ processing. This is not handled correctly and may lead to defeating the RPZ rule. It also may lead to an unexpected exit of the BIND 9 software. This issue affects BIND 9 versions 9.16.0 through 9.18.50, 9.20.0 through 9.20.24, 9.21.0 through 9.21.23, 9.16.8-S1 through 9.18.50-S1, and 9.20.9-S1 through 9.20.24-S1. (CVE-2026-11331)
cves.impact: This vulnerability allows an unauthenticated denial-of-service (DoS) when BIND processes a DNS query that matches a Response Policy Zone (RPZ) configured with wildcard CNAME policies. An attacker who knows or guesses that the resolver uses RPZ with wildcard CNAME policies can craft query names long enough to trigger a NAMETOOLONG error condition during RPZ processing. This error is not handled correctly and may lead to defeating the RPZ rule and an unexpected exit of the named process, causing a DoS. An RPZ configured with wildcard CNAME policies is a standard, GUI-configured DNS firewall feature of BIG-IP DNS, documented in the BIG-IP DNS Services: Implementations guide.
cves.mitigation:
To mitigate this issue, do not configure RPZ with wildcard CNAME policies until a patched BIND is applied; or disable the Use BIND Server in the DNS profile.

Disable the Use BIND Server on BIG-IP option in the DNS profile

Important: Disabling the BIND server can affect DNS configurations that use BIND as a fallback method (return to DNS) for resolution.

Log in to the Configuration utility.
Go to Local Traffic > Profiles > Services > DNS.
Select the applicable DNS profile.
For Use BIND Server on BIG-IP, select Disabled.
Select Update.

Statement from www.php.net:
We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector. This setting was already listed as a mitigation in the GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp advisory for CVE-2026-109619 published on Oct 21st, 2026. If you applied it then, keep it in place and no further action is needed.
The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled. Since this setup is unlikely in practice, we are handling it in the regular release cycle and will publish a full advisory for CVE-2026-115560 with the next release. (CVE-2026-115560)

BIG-IP mitigation

The following mitigates BIG-IP control plane configuration utility exposure as well as BIG-IP APM data plane exposure. If you applied the mitigation from K000163821: PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, then session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 is already configured and you don't need to perform the following mitigation.

At a high level, the admin needs to login on BIG-IP with advanced shell, create a new file with the content below, and restart apache.

Important: F5 recommends that you verify the following php.ini configuration in your testing/staging environment before deploying to your production environment.

Note: If you have a multi bladed system these steps must be done on each individual blade.

Create a new file - /etc/php.ini.d/K000163878.ini and include the content below.

; The configuration mitigations recommended by PHP for CVE-2026-115560 
; These will NOT survive an upgrade of BIG-IP TMOS. 
session.upload_progress.enabled = 0

Restart apache using bigstart restart httpd.

On multi-bladed systems, restart apache using clsh bigstart restart httpd.

Only for BIG-IP APM systems, restart apache using bigstart restart httpd_sam.

On multi-bladed BIG-IP APM restart apache using clsh bigstart restart httpd_sam.

Note: Restarting the httpd_sam process may disrupt webtop connections, requiring users to reconnect.

If you have configured a device group, repeat on each high availability (HA) peer in the group.

cves.description: CVE-2026-11999 X.509 trust-chain bypass (path-depth exhaustion) in the OpenSSL compatibility certificate verifier (wolfSSL_X509_verify_cert()). This affects only builds with --enable-opensslextra whose application calls X509_verify_cert() with caller-supplied untrusted intermediates; for those users it is critical, otherwise the library is unaffected.
